description_full: General Motors Company designs, builds, and sells trucks, crossovers, cars, and automobile parts worldwide. It operates through GM North America, GM International, and GM Financial segments. The company markets its vehicles primarily under the Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC, Baojun, and Wuling brand names. In addition, it sells trucks, crossovers, cars, and automobile parts through retail dealers, distributors and dealers, as well as to fleet customers, including daily rental car companies, commercial fleet customers, leasing companies, and governments. Further, the company offers various range of after-sale services through dealer network, such as maintenance, light repairs, collision repairs, vehicle accessories, and extended service warranties. Additionally, it provides automotive financing; and software-enabled services and subscriptions. General Motors Company was founded in 1908 and is based in Detroit, Michigan.

financial_summary: General Motors Company Common Stock is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $66.4B market cap on $185.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 24% against a 11% cost of capital — a 13-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $17.6B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 9.96× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 10.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin trails the Consumer Cyclical median (8%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.

Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-26.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 380 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 14% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 1.19, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.76 vs 5y 1.25), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $562.6M traded a day.

val: The stock trades 73% below its DCF fair value of $291, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 83%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $220 to $392 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/FCF 3.8 vs 15.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 456% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 26.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $101 on average, 29% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 24% clears the cost of capital of 11.2% by 13pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.20).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 4% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.6% of revenue on R&D and 0.2% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $27.7B (32% of market cap).
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.20 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.7% over 3 years, 8.6% over 5 years and 2.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 18% of profits supports about 4.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 19%.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (5.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (29 sales, net $106.2M sold).
It returns 10.0% a year to shareholders (9.1% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 10.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 156,000 employees, each generates about $1.2M of revenue, 3.1x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $113K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.3M (7x revenue per employee).
